covent: The covered piazza of Covent Garden with its street performers, then the lanes of Soho: Neal's Yard, the courtyard of colourful façades, Chinatown with its red lanterns and Carnaby Street.
trafalgar: Trafalgar Square and the National Gallery
The great square with Nelson's Column and the bronze lions; on the north side the National Gallery, with Van Gogh, Leonardo, Turner and Botticelli. At the end of Whitehall you can glimpse Big Ben.
westminster: The Palace of Westminster with its clock tower ("Big Ben" is actually the bell), Westminster Bridge with the view of the London Eye and, opposite Parliament, Westminster Abbey, where kings are crowned.
buckingham: Buckingham Palace and St James's Park

The King's palace with the Victoria Memorial in front and The Mall, the red avenue leading to Trafalgar Square. Next door is St James's Park, with its lake, the pelicans and a view of the palace from a little bridge.
stpaul: St Paul's Cathedral and Millennium Bridge
Christopher Wren's dome, one of the largest in the world, above the entrance steps; from there you walk down to the Millennium Bridge, the footbridge that takes you to Tate Modern in a minute.
southbank: A walk along the Thames: Tate Modern, the former power station with its Turbine Hall, Shakespeare's Globe and the bridges, with the City opposite.
borough: London's oldest covered market, with stalls of cheese, bread, spices and street food, next to Southwark Cathedral and London Bridge.
towerbridge: Tower Bridge and the Tower of London from outside
Walk across the Victorian bascule bridge, with the Tower of London on the north side and views of the Shard and the Thames. The best shots are from the Potters Fields riverside on the south bank.
abbeyins: The Abbey where English kings have been crowned since 1066: the tomb of Elizabeth I, Poets' Corner and the cloisters. Outside, the Palace of Westminster with the Big Ben tower and Westminster Bridge.
stpaulins: Wren's cathedral with its 111-metre dome: the Whispering Gallery, where a whisper carries to the other side, the crypt with the tombs of Nelson and Wellington and, if your legs allow, the climb to the Golden Gallery for the view.
toweroflondon: William the Conqueror's fortress: the Crown Jewels, the White Tower with its armour, the walls overlooking the river and the guided tour by the Yeoman Warders (the "Beefeaters"), included in the ticket.
british: The Rosetta Stone, the Parthenon marbles, the Egyptian mummies and the glass-roofed Great Court: two hours are enough for the masterpieces, seeing it all would take days.
museums: South Kensington: Natural History and V&A

The Natural History Museum, in a Romanesque-style palace with a blue whale skeleton in the great entrance hall, and opposite the Victoria and Albert Museum, with decorative arts, fashion and jewellery from all over the world.
kensington: A walk through the great central park: the Serpentine lake, Kensington Gardens, the Sunken Garden and the façade of the palace where Diana lived.
notting: The pastel houses of Notting Hill, the streets around Lancaster Road and Portobello Road, with its antique stalls, vintage shops and colourful façades.
camden: The Camden Lock and Stables markets, the canal with its locks and alternative shops, then along Regent's Canal to Primrose Hill, the hill with a view of the London skyline.
eastend: Brick Lane with its murals and curry houses, the covered Old Spitalfields Market and the streets of Shoreditch full of street art.
greenwich: The village on the Thames with the Cutty Sark clipper, the covered market, the Queen's House and, at the top of the hill in Greenwich Park, the Royal Observatory, where the Prime Meridian runs.
eye: The observation wheel on the south bank of the Thames, with views of Big Ben and Parliament. A ride takes about 30 minutes.
